B1:
Cause: Touched fires once per touching part and repeatedly as limbs make contact (feet, legs, HumanoidRootPart...), often several times in the same frame. part:Destroy() doesn't stop handlers already queued, so several Touched events run before the part is gone; each adds 10. There is no debounce. (Also: if this ran on the client it wouldn't replicate; keep it server-side.)
Fix: guard with a debounce flag set before granting:
```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local part = script.Parent
local collected = false
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    if collected then return end
    local char = hit:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
    local plr = char and Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(char)
    if not plr then return end
    local hum = char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end
    collected = true -- set before anything else
    local coins = plr:FindFirstChild("leaderstats") and plr.leaderstats:FindFirstChild("Coins")
    if coins then coins.Value += 10 end
    part:Destroy()
end)
```
For respawning coins, use a per-coin flag or per-player table and reset after the cooldown; for many coins, one tag-driven CollectionService script.
B2:
With StreamingEnabled, the client only has instances near the player (within the streaming radius). Far doors aren't streamed in when the LocalScript runs (and can be streamed out later), so indexing `.Door` directly errors; the path Hotel exists (maybe as an empty/partial model) but Door doesn't.
Fix 1: wait for it with a timeout and handle nil/stream-out:
```lua
local hotel = workspace:WaitForChild("Map"):WaitForChild("Buildings"):WaitForChild("Hotel")
local door = hotel:WaitForChild("Door", 10)
if door then door.Touched:Connect(onTouch) end
```
(also listen for it being removed/re-added; set the Hotel model's ModelStreamingMode = Atomic so children arrive together, or Persistent if it must always exist - use sparingly.)
Fix 2 (preferred for many doors): tag doors with CollectionService ("Door") and use GetTagged + GetInstanceAddedSignal / GetInstanceRemovedSignal so each door is wired when it streams in and cleaned up when it streams out. Better still, detect door touches on the server (which always has every instance) and only do visuals on the client.
B3:
Bugs:
1. Always returns PurchaseGranted, even when pcall fails (ok ignored) -> charged, nothing given, Roblox never retries.
2. plr may be nil (player left); plr.UserId errors inside pcall -> swallowed -> Granted with nothing given. Use info.PlayerId, or return NotProcessedYet.
3. Not idempotent: no PurchaseId check. Roblox re-calls ProcessReceipt for unacknowledged receipts (errors, timeouts, server shutdown, retries), so coins can be granted twice.
4. GetAsync + SetAsync is a non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent writes from another server/autosave lose or double coins. Also likely conflicts with the session-managed player save (two writers to the same data).
5. Doesn't update the in-game balance for the online player.
Correct behaviour: one ProcessReceipt for the whole game; look up handler by info.ProductId; UpdateAsync on the player's data (or the session-locked profile) that, inside the transform, returns nil/no change if info.PurchaseId is already in a recorded purchase list, else adds 100 coins and records the PurchaseId (cap list size); return PurchaseGranted only after that save succeeded (or the PurchaseId was already recorded); return NotProcessedYet on any failure, unknown product or if the player isn't in this server/data not loaded, so Roblox retries later. Then update the live value.
B4:
Remote arguments are serialized: tables are copied as plain data, metatables are stripped, and functions can't be sent. So the client gets {Name="Rifle", Ammo=30} with no __index -> w:Fire is nil -> "attempt to call a nil value". (Mixed/non-string keys and cyclic tables also get mangled.)
Instances are sent as references; the client receives nil if that instance doesn't exist/replicate on the client. ServerStorage never replicates to clients, so Muzzle is nil (same for server-only or not-yet-streamed instances).
Fix: send plain data and rebuild the object on the client with a shared class module in ReplicatedStorage:
```lua
-- server
remote:FireClient(plr, { Name = w.Name, Ammo = w.Ammo }, "Muzzle")
-- client
local Weapon = require(ReplicatedStorage.Shared.Weapon)
remote.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(data, muzzleName)
    local w = Weapon.new(data) -- setmetatable on the client
    local muzzle = ReplicatedStorage.Assets:FindFirstChild(muzzleName)
end)
```
Put assets the client needs in ReplicatedStorage (or clone into workspace / the player's PlayerGui) and send their name/id, or reference an instance that replicates.
B5:
workspace:Raycast's direction is a displacement vector, not a unit direction: its length is the ray's max distance. .Unit makes the ray only 1 stud long, so it nearly never reaches anything. Also, starting at the shooter's head/gun, the ray may hit the shooter's own character/gun first.
Fix:
```lua
local MAX_RANGE = 500
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * MAX_RANGE -- or just target - origin to stop at target
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = { shooterCharacter }
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
Validate target/origin on the server (origin near the shooter, NaN checks) for hitscan security.
B6:
When the last player leaves, the server starts shutting down; PlayerRemoving fires but the server may close before the async SetAsync completes (the game doesn't wait for running threads), so the save is lost. Same on Roblox-initiated shutdowns (updates, "shut down all servers").
Standard fix: game:BindToClose: on close, save every still-loaded player and wait for all saves to finish (up to the ~30-second limit), running them in parallel with task.spawn and a counter/wait. Track per-player "saving/saved" so PlayerRemoving and BindToClose don't double-save, and use UpdateAsync with session locking instead of blind SetAsync. Add periodic autosaves (every few minutes) so a crash loses little. In Studio, skip or shorten BindToClose saves if needed (RunService:IsStudio()).
```lua
game:BindToClose(function()
    local pending = 0
    for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
        pending += 1
        task.spawn(function() savePlayer(p, true); pending -= 1 end)
    end
    while pending > 0 do task.wait() end
end)
```

local lastUse: { [Player]: number } = {}

UseAbility.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player: Player, abilityId)

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local MPS = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local DSS = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DSS:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local GEMS100 = 123456

			data.receipts = data.receipts or {}

```lua
local TeleportService = game:GetService("TeleportService")
local MAX_ATTEMPTS, RETRY_DELAY = 4, 2

local function safeTeleport(placeId: number, players: { Player }, teleportData: any?)
	local options = Instance.new("TeleportOptions")
	if teleportData ~= nil then options:SetTeleportData(teleportData) end
	for attempt = 1, MAX_ATTEMPTS do
		local ok, result = pcall(TeleportService.TeleportAsync, TeleportService, placeId, players, options)
		if ok then return true, result end
		warn(("Teleport attempt %d failed: %s"):format(attempt, tostring(result)))
		task.wait(RETRY_DELAY * attempt)
	end
	return false
end

-- TeleportAsync can succeed initially and fail later per player
local retries: { [Player]: number } = {}
TeleportService.TeleportInitFailed:Connect(function(player, result, message, placeId, options)
	if result == Enum.TeleportResult.Unauthorized or result == Enum.TeleportResult.IsTeleporting then
		return -- not retryable / already in progress
	end
	local n = (retries[player] or 0) + 1
	retries[player] = n
	if n > 3 then retries[player] = nil; warn("Giving up on", player.Name, message) return end
	task.wait(RETRY_DELAY)
	if player.Parent then
		pcall(TeleportService.TeleportAsync, TeleportService, placeId, { player }, options)
	end
end)
game:GetService("Players").PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(p) retries[p] = nil end)
```

B13:
(a) Buying: client -> server RemoteEvent (e.g. BuySword, sending only the itemId). Optionally a RemoteFunction client->server if the client wants a success/failure reply, but the server must not trust anything else. Validation (item exists, price from server config, balance, rate limit) and the coin balance live on the server (server-owned data/leaderstats, saved by the server).
(b) Counter update: server -> client RemoteEvent (FireClient with the new balance), or simply a replicated value the client watches (leaderstats IntValue / player attribute with GetAttributeChangedSignal). The client only displays; it never sets the balance.
Why not RemoteFunction:InvokeClient for UI: the server would yield until the client returns. A malicious or lagging client can never return (hanging the server thread forever), error, or return garbage, and if the client leaves mid-invoke it errors. Displaying a value needs no reply, so a one-way event/replicated value is simpler and safe. Roblox docs warn against InvokeClient for this reason.
B14:
Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData / GetJoinData on arrival) travels through the client, so it's readable and spoofable by exploiters, has size limits, and is lost if the teleport fails or the player rejoins differently. Fine only for non-authoritative hints (chosen map, party id, UI state) - and the loadout choice could go there only if the server validates it against what the player owns.
DataStores: authoritative, persistent; save before teleport (with session locking, release the lock so the destination can load) and load in the match place. Slower, consumes budget, and the save/load race across teleport must be handled (session lock with retry).
MemoryStores (HashMap/SortedMap): fast, cross-server, ephemeral with expiry; good for transient handoff like the selected loadout or match assignment keyed by UserId, but not durable storage.
Choice: coin balance stays in the DataStore (session-locked player profile) - the source of truth, never in teleport data. Loadout: store in the player's DataStore profile (or a MemoryStore HashMap entry with short TTL for the session), optionally mirror its id in teleport data as a hint, and always validate server-side in the match place against owned items. Save and wait for completion before calling TeleportAsync.
B16:
Ownership: give the driver's client network ownership of the car's assembly (vehicle:SetNetworkOwner(driverPlayer) when they sit in the VehicleSeat; Roblox's auto ownership typically does this for the seat occupant). Physics then simulates on the driver, so steering is responsive with no input latency. When no one drives, return ownership to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) or auto.
Risk: the owning client is authoritative over that assembly's physics. An exploiter can teleport the car, set any velocity (speed hacks), fly, noclip through walls, skip checkpoints, or ram/fling other players; anything welded to it is also client-controlled.
Server must still validate: speed/acceleration vs the car's max (sample position over time), teleport/position jumps, checkpoints passed in order with plausible times (lap time minimum), that the car stays on/near the track, finish line results and rewards (computed server-side), and anything gameplay-critical like collisions/damage, boosts and item use (validate cooldowns and ownership). On violations, reset the car, take back ownership, or flag. Don't trust client-sent lap times or positions via remotes. Alternative: Server Authority mode (AuthorityMode = Server) gives predicted, server-authoritative physics without client ownership trust.
B17:
Use an UnreliableRemoteEvent (and lower/adaptive send rate, e.g. 10-20 Hz with client-side interpolation, sending only when aim changes). Aim/position is continuous state where only the latest value matters, so dropped or reordered packets are fine and you avoid the reliable queue's head-of-line blocking/backlog.
Constraints and handling:
- Unreliable: packets may be dropped -> send absolute state (not deltas), and interpolate/extrapolate on receivers.
- Unordered: packets may arrive out of order -> include a sequence number or timestamp and ignore older ones.
- Payload size limit (~1,000 bytes per call; larger payloads are dropped) -> keep packets small: quantize (e.g. pack yaw/pitch into int16s, position as Vector3int16 or relative offsets) and pack with buffer.
- Not for critical events (shots fired, hits, purchases) -> keep those on reliable RemoteEvents.
- Still rate-limit and validate on the server (NaN, plausible speeds/angles), since exploiters can spam it.
- Throttles exist per player; batch multiple values into one call per tick rather than many calls.
Also consider whether the server needs it at all: character position already replicates via physics; only send aim (2 numbers).
B18:
Parallel Luau: split NPCs across several Actors (e.g. 4-16, each owning a batch of NPC models/scripts, or a pool of worker Actors you send work to with Actor:SendMessage). In each Actor, run the per-NPC work in parallel: RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel(fn) or task.desynchronize(), do the read-only parts (workspace:Raycast, spatial queries, path scoring math, target selection), then task.synchronize() and apply results serially (move, set properties, fire remotes, change state). Spread work over frames (time-slice: not every NPC every Heartbeat) and raycast less often.
Limitations to design around:
- In the parallel phase you cannot write most Instance properties, create/destroy/reparent instances, or call many yielding/thread-unsafe APIs; writes must be deferred to the serial phase (task.synchronize).
- Each Actor is a separate Luau VM: module state isn't shared; requires run separately per Actor; communicate via SendMessage/BindToMessage(Parallel) or SharedTable (copies/locks cost).
- Instances an Actor modifies should be descendants of that Actor (safe to modify only its own subtree).
- Data passed between actors is copied (no functions/metatables), so keep messages small.
- Overhead: too many tiny actors or sync/desync per NPC cost more than they save; batch.
- Results aren't deterministic in ordering; avoid races on shared state.
- Benefit depends on server cores; profile with MicroProfiler/ScriptProfiler. PathfindingService ComputeAsync isn't a parallel API - cache paths, recompute rarely.
B19:
Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled so clients only load nearby content. Sensible settings: StreamingMinRadius ~64 (default 64) and StreamingTargetRadius ~1024 by default; for mobile-heavy open worlds you may lower target to ~512-768 with min 64-128; StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic (stream out far content proactively, helps memory) and StreamingIntegrityMode = MinimumRadiusPause/PauseOutsideLoadedArea so players don't fall into unloaded areas. Per model, set ModelStreamingMode: Default/Nonatomic for scenery, Atomic for models whose parts must arrive together (doors, NPCs, vehicles), Persistent only for few essential things (spawn, global landmarks), PersistentPerPlayer + AddPersistentPlayer for player-specific needs. Large distant landmarks: low-detail far models or rely on LoD (ModelLevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh for imposters).
Scripts: client code can no longer assume everything exists. Replace direct paths (workspace.Map.X.Y) with WaitForChild with timeouts, nil checks, and CollectionService GetInstanceAddedSignal/RemovedSignal to set up/tear down per instance as it streams in/out. Keep authoritative logic on the server (which has everything). Use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(position) before teleporting a player, and LocalPlayer.ReplicationFocus considerations for cameras far from the character. Test with Studio's streaming emulation and on low-memory devices.
B20:
Cause: 80 players x every 5 s = 960 SetAsync per minute, plus a per-key write rate (a key written every 5 s; the old guideline was >= 6 s between writes to the same key). Per-server write budget is ~60 + 10 x players per minute (here ~860) and each key's write throughput is limited, so requests pile into the DataStore queue; when the queue fills (30 queued requests for a key/request type), new requests are dropped with error 302 (SetAsync request dropped, queue full) and saves are lost. SetAsync also blindly overwrites, risking rollbacks.
Better design: keep data in memory (session-cached profile) and save only: on PlayerRemoving, in BindToClose, and autosave every ~1-5 minutes per player, staggered (spread players across the interval) and only if the data changed (dirty flag). Use UpdateAsync with session locking, pcall with exponential backoff, and check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before writing (defer if low). Save immediately only for important events (purchases via ProcessReceipt). For high-frequency shared data, use MemoryStores. Since 2026 budgets are per experience (writes 300 + 20 x CCU per minute), still well over a 5-second loop at scale.

B22:
The Input Action System (IAS; full release June 2026) has three core instances:
- InputContext: a group of actions you enable/disable and prioritise (Enabled, Priority, Sink). Contexts can be swapped (gameplay, menu, vehicle).
- InputAction: one abstract action, with Type (Bool, Direction1D, Direction2D, Direction3D, ViewportPosition). Read via GetState(); signals Pressed and Released (for Bool) and StateChanged (any type).
- InputBinding: maps a physical input to its parent action: KeyCode (keyboard, mouse, gamepad), modifiers (PrimaryModifier/SecondaryModifier for chords), UIButton for touch buttons, Scale/vector settings for directional composites. Give each action keyboard/mouse, gamepad and touch bindings.
Signalling a press: for a Bool action, when a bound input goes down the action's state becomes true and Pressed fires (StateChanged(true)); release fires Released.
Menu precedence: put menu actions in their own InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay/default player-script contexts and Sink = true, so inputs bound in the menu context are consumed and don't reach lower-priority contexts (movement/jump); enable it when the menu opens and disable it on close (or disable the gameplay context). The default player scripts use IAS contexts when Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem is Enabled. (Server Authority and Input Migration 2026)
B23:
Roblox's engine UI styling (similar to CSS):
- StyleSheet: holds StyleRules (and token attributes).
- StyleRule: a Selector plus property overrides set with StyleRule:SetProperties({...}); rules can nest. Selectors match class names (Frame, TextButton), tags (".Tag" via CollectionService), instance names ("#Name"), state pseudo-classes (":hover" etc. via GuiState), phantom children like UICorner/UIStroke added by the rule ("::UICorner"), and queries prefixed @.
- StyleLink: links a StyleSheet to a ScreenGui (or other UI root) so its rules apply to that tree (one sheet per tree).
- StyleDerive: makes one sheet inherit another (e.g. a theme/token sheet).
- StyleQuery: conditional rules (MaxSize, PreferredInput, accessibility), e.g. @ViewportDisplaySizeSmall, @PreferredInputTouch.
- Studio Style Editor (beta) edits this visually.
How styles reach UI: a StyleLink under the ScreenGui points at the sheet; the engine matches rules' selectors against instances in that tree and applies the property overrides (higher-priority/more specific rules win), live as instances change.
Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (e.g. tokens:SetAttribute("Primary", Color3...)); derive it into the main sheet with StyleDerive; rules reference the token as a string "$Primary" (BackgroundColor3 = "$Primary"). Swapping the token sheet (themes with same token names) restyles everything. (UI Design Systems)
B24:
Method: an age check, typically facial age estimation (via the Roblox app camera, run by a vendor; images not stored), with government ID verification or parental controls able to correct the estimate. Required for chat from late 2025/January 2026 globally.
Age groups (as reported): under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20, 21+. (Roblox platform audiences in 2026: Kids 5-8, Select 9-15, Roblox 16+.)
Restriction: age-based chat lets users chat only with their own age group and the groups directly above and below (e.g. 9-12 can chat with under-9 and 13-15), designed to stop children under 16 from communicating with adults. Under-9s need parental consent for chat (Kids accounts have communication off by default). Trusted Connections let age-checked 13+ users chat more freely with people they know beyond adjacent groups. Users who haven't completed the check can't use chat. In-game, messages simply don't appear to players outside the allowed groups, so gameplay must not depend on chat (use system messages via DisplaySystemMessage, non-chat UI). There is no developer API returning a player's age group. (Age Checks and Safety Features)
